sysd-found-130.title: System design: choices that are hard to undo
sysd-found-130.text: The choices a team makes earliest are the ones it is least able to take back. System design is the process of defining the architecture, interfaces and data of a system so that it satisfies specific requirements. It is one of the earliest decisions made when building a system, and high-level design decisions are very difficult to correct later. That is why it is essential to think from a high level early on. The goal is a system that is scalable, reliable and efficient, and that meets the needs of a business or organization through a systematic approach to building it. Good design means thinking about everything, from the infrastructure all the way down to the data and how it is stored. The study of it is the study of a system's component parts and how they interact with one another. The scope is wide. It starts with the requirements a system must meet, covered in {{ref:sysd-found-207}} and {{ref:sysd-found-139}}. It runs through the choice of data store, the ways of scaling up and out, and the passing of messages between parts. It ends with watching a running system and automating how it is built, tested and deployed. A clear design pays off again later, because it makes architectural changes easier to reason about and manage as the system evolves.

sysd-found-131.title: System design interview: no single right answer
sysd-found-131.text: There is no answer key for a system design interview. It evaluates a candidate's ability to produce technical solutions to abstract problems, so it is not designed for one specific answer. The questions are vague or abstract by nature, and the topic is very extensive. The interview is also unusual, because it runs both ways between the candidate and the interviewer. Expectations differ at each engineering level, since an experienced engineer approaches the problem differently from someone new, which is why no single strategy keeps every candidate organized. One practical tip comes from Singh: read the engineering blog of the company you are interviewing with, to learn its technology stack and which problems matter to it. The subject being tested is system design itself, covered in {{ref:sysd-found-130}}.

sysd-found-136.title: System design building blocks: six categories
sysd-found-136.text: Large systems look different from one another, yet they are assembled from the same standard pieces. The building blocks of system design are those components, grouped into six broad categories. Distributed computing comes first. Its blocks are a queue of messages that lets services communicate asynchronously and stay decoupled. Next come a cache spread across machines, which keeps frequently accessed data in memory, and a task scheduler that coordinates running tasks. Scaling and performance is the second category. It holds scaling services that adjust capacity to demand and CDNs that serve content from geographically closer locations. It also holds a hashing scheme that minimizes key remapping when nodes join or leave, covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-078}}. Service management is the way services find and talk to each other without hard-coded network locations, covered in {{ref:sysd-msg-092}}. Networking and communication brings DNS, which maps domain names to network addresses. It also brings a load balancer that spreads incoming traffic across servers, and a single entry point for a group of services, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-133}}. Data storage and management covers stores for structured data and storage for images, videos and documents. It also covers sharding, which partitions data across nodes, and copying data to multiple nodes, which scales the store. The sixth category, observing the system and keeping it resilient, means gaining insight into its internal state through metrics, logging and tracing.

sysd-found-207.title: Functional requirements: what the system must do
sysd-found-207.text: Every system begins as a list of things it must do. A functional requirement defines a function of a system or component as behavior between inputs and outputs, a statement of what the system is supposed to accomplish. It is usually written 'system shall do <requirement>', for one individual action or part of the system. Functional requirements drive the application architecture, and they are planned in the system design, covered in {{ref:sysd-found-130}}. A good specification gives each one a unique name and number, a brief summary, a rationale, the required behavior and references to related use cases.

sysd-found-139.title: Non-functional requirements: how the system must be
sysd-found-139.text: A system can do everything on its list and still fail. A system's overall properties commonly mark the difference between a development project succeeding or failing. A non-functional requirement specifies criteria for judging how a system operates, an overall property such as availability or performance, rather than a specific behavior. Where a functional requirement says what the system shall do, a non-functional one says what it shall be. Each should be stated in a specific and measurable way. These requirements go by many names, including quality attributes, qualities, constraints and, informally, the 'ilities'. Execution qualities such as safety, security and usability show at run time. Evolution qualities such as testability, maintainability and extensibility live in the static structure of the system. In an interview they sound like a demand that every request be processed with the minimum delay, or that the system be highly available.

sysd-found-138.title: Software architecture: the blueprint behind a system
sysd-found-138.text: A blueprint is cheap to change on paper and costly to change once the building stands. Software architecture works the same way. It is the set of structures needed to reason about a software system, and the discipline of creating them. Each structure comprises software elements, the relations among them, and properties of both. The architecture is about fundamental structural choices that are costly to change once implemented. It shapes the infrastructure in which the functionality runs, so that the system's non-functional requirements are met. Two fundamental laws of software architecture are that everything is a trade-off and that why is more important than how. As an abstraction a team can grasp, it lets people analyse a system's behavior before it is built, saving cost and risk. Architectures fall into two main types, monolith and distributed, and tend to become more complex over time.

sysd-found-137.title: Common scaling problems and their standard fixes
sysd-found-137.text: Large systems tend to break in the same few places, and each place has a standard remedy. Eight problems recur in production. A read-heavy system is helped by a cache, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-001}}. High write traffic goes to async workers that process the writes, or to data stores powered by LSM-trees. A part whose failure would stop the whole system is removed with redundant copies of critical components, such as the data store. A mechanism that switches over when one copy fails completes the fix. To keep a service available, a load balancer sends requests only to healthy server instances. Copying the data store to other machines improves availability and protects the data from loss. A long delay before a response arrives is reduced with a CDN, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-069}}. Large files and complex data go to block and object stores, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-143}} and {{ref:sysd-blocks-145}}. Watching a system and raising alerts relies on a centralized logging system, for example the ELK stack. Slow queries are fixed with proper indexes and by sharding to scale the data store horizontally.

sysd-found-142.title: Architecture decision records: writing the why down
sysd-found-142.text: A decision nobody wrote down tends to be argued again and again. Forgotten, undocumented or misunderstood decisions, often those communicated by email, cause repeated discussions without resolution. Architecture decision records are the remedy: single, accessible records that capture each architectural decision with its technical and business justification. Architects usually record both, often about cost, user satisfaction and time to market, in one record kept in an accessible repository such as a wiki. That gives a single, updated source of truth. The records also help the architect who fears choosing wrongly and delays: deciding at the 'last responsible moment', in close collaboration with the development team, avoids analysis paralysis.

sysd-found-141.title: Software architecture activities: four steps, repeated
sysd-found-141.text: Nobody finishes an architecture in one pass. Software architecture design consists of four core activities, analysis, synthesis, evaluation and evolution, carried out iteratively at different stages of development. Analysis understands the environment of a proposed system and determines its requirements. Its outputs are the architecturally significant requirements, those with a measurable impact on the architecture. Synthesis creates and improves the design from them, and evaluation determines how well the current design satisfies them, for example with the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method. Evolution maintains and adapts an existing architecture to changing requirements. Supporting activities run throughout: knowledge management, design reasoning and documentation.
